questions.title: Why does the Federal Circuit review DuPont factor findings for “substantial evidence” but the ultimate likelihood-of-confusion question de novo?
questions.question_body: The opinion says each DuPont factor is a fact question reviewed for substantial evidence, but likelihood of confusion is a legal question reviewed de novo. I'm struggling to understand where the line is drawn. For example, when the Board decides the services are “highly similar,” is that a factual finding insulated by substantial evidence review, while the weight that similarity gets in the overall confusion analysis is legal? How does this framework affect what arguments can win on appeal from the TTAB?

questions.title: How should the sixth DuPont factor’s “similar goods” be defined when the second factor already found services to be highly similar or partially legally identical?
questions.question_body: The court faults the Board for narrowing the sixth factor to only credit card services, given it had already found Apex’s ‘banking and financing services’ highly similar and partially legally identical to CC Serve’s ‘credit card services’ under the second factor. Do courts require the scope of ‘similar goods/services’ for third-party-use evidence (factor six) to match the scope used for relatedness (factor two)? Are there limits to how broadly you can cast ‘similar goods’ under factor six, and how do Olde Tyme Foods, Juice Generation, and Jack Wolfskin guide that line-drawing?

questions.title: What evidentiary showing is needed under factor six to prove a mark is commercially weak—are registrations enough, or is marketplace use required?
questions.question_body: The Board counted nine Aspire-formative marks for credit card services and said that wasn’t ‘considerable’ compared to other cases with 14 or 26 examples. On remand, if Apex can include 42 additional Aspire uses in broader banking/finance, how does the Board weigh registrations versus actual use? Does the Federal Circuit require proof of marketplace use to show consumer conditioning, or can a critical mass of third-party registrations alone demonstrate conceptual weakness?

questions.title: Was it proper for the Board to treat ‘credit card services’ and ‘banking and financing services’ as legally identical in part, especially given the deletion of ‘credit card services’ from the ID Manual?
questions.question_body: The Board defined the legacy ‘credit card services’ identification to include issuing cards, processing, authorization, account management, etc., and then used dictionary definitions of ‘banking’ and ‘finance’ to find partial legal identity with Apex’s services. Is this consistent with TTAB precedent on construing older IDs when the ID Manual has changed? What sources can the Board rely on to interpret an existing registration’s scope, and how much overlap is necessary to say services are ‘legally identical, in part’?

questions.title: How does commercial strength under factor six affect the first DuPont factor’s ‘commercial impression’ analysis of the marks themselves?
questions.question_body: The court vacated the first factor because revisiting factor six might change the mark’s commercial strength and thus the overall commercial impression. I thought the first factor focuses on appearance, sound, and connotation of the marks. In practice, how does the perceived strength/weakness of the cited mark change the first-factor analysis? Is strength normally treated under factor six only, or does it permeate factor one as part of ‘commercial impression’?

questions.title: Does CC Serve’s role as a program manager partnering with issuing banks matter for the relatedness of services under factor two?
questions.question_body: Apex argued CC Serve doesn’t ‘provide banking services’ but partners with banks to manage ASPIRE credit card programs. The court called that unavailing. In likelihood-of-confusion analysis, does it matter that the opposer is not itself a bank if it offers card-related services closely tied to banking? How do tribunals treat distinctions between issuers, servicers, and program managers when the identifications of services—and consumer perception of source—overlap?

questions.title: On remand, is the Board limited to reconsidering only factors one and six, and can it take new evidence or must it decide on the existing record?
questions.question_body: The Federal Circuit affirmed the second factor but vacated and remanded as to the sixth and first factors. Procedurally, is the TTAB confined to the current record when reevaluating third-party use and commercial impression, or can it reopen the record for additional evidence? Also, is the Board precluded from revisiting the second factor’s relatedness findings, or can new sixth-factor analysis indirectly affect how much weight it gives other factors?
